# Model Summary

LoRA adapter for employment-scam detection in job advertisements, fine-tuned on
**Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1** (46.7B total parameters, 12.9B active per token —
sparse mixture-of-experts) via [Adaption's](https://adaptionlabs.ai)
AutoScientist platform. Given a job advertisement, the model answers with one
word: `LEGITIMATE` or `FRAUDULENT`.

The task is **binary classification at a 4.84% base rate**. That base rate is the
whole difficulty: always answering `LEGITIMATE` scores 95.2% accuracy and F1
**0.000** on the class that matters. Accuracy is not reported anywhere in this
card; precision and recall on the fraudulent class are.

Submitted to the **AutoScientist Challenge 2026** (HR category).

> **Holdout performance has not been measured.** The training run converged
> (final train loss 0.0030, eval loss 0.0243) and the LoRA weights carry a real
> update, but recall and false-positive rate on the held-out set are not yet
> known. **Do not deploy this model.** See *Evaluation Results*.

## Usage

This is a LoRA adapter. Load it on top of the base model using PEFT.

Note that the distributed archive is **zstd-compressed despite the `.tgz`
extension** — extract with `tar --use-compress-program=unzstd -xf`, not `tar -xzf`.

```python
import torch
from peft import PeftModel
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

base = "mistralai/Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(base)
base_model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    base, torch_dtype=torch.float16, device_map="auto",
)
model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(
    base_model,
    "/kaggle/input/emscad-employment-scam-detection-adapter/other/default/1",
)

# The exact prompt the adapter was trained on. The stated base rate is part of
# it: removing that sentence changes the model's operating point.
PROMPT = """You are reviewing a job advertisement submitted to an applicant tracking system, to decide whether it is a legitimate posting or an employment scam.

Employment scams typically aim to harvest personal data or money from applicants. Roughly 5% of postings in this system are fraudulent, so most ads you see are legitimate.

Answer with exactly one word: LEGITIMATE or FRAUDULENT. Nothing else.

JOB ADVERTISEMENT:
{text}"""

ad = (
    "Title: Data Entry Clerk\n\n"
    "Description: Work from home, no experience needed. Earn $500/week "
    "processing simple forms. Immediate start, flexible hours. Send your "
    "details to begin training today."
)

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT.format(text=ad)}]
inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages, add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device)
outputs = model.generate(inputs, max_new_tokens=8, do_sample=False)
print(tokenizer.decode(outputs[0][inputs.shape[-1]:], skip_special_tokens=True))
```

**Input:** A job advertisement as plain text — title, company profile,
description, requirements, benefits. **Text only:** see *Known limitations*.
**Output:** One word, `LEGITIMATE` or `FRAUDULENT`.

**Known limitations:**

- **Holdout recall and false-positive rate are unmeasured.** This is the
  headline limitation, not a footnote.
- **Text-only by design.** EMSCAD ships metadata columns (`has_company_logo`,
  `has_questions`, `telecommuting`) that leak the label: the single rule
  `no logo → fraud` scores F1 0.258 on its own, rivalling the published Random
  Forest that used them. This adapter never sees those flags. A model that needs
  them is doing tabular classification on three binary features, not reading an
  advertisement.
- **Vocabulary is 2012–2014.** EMSCAD ads predate remote-work normalization,
  and scam patterns have moved on since.
- **Automated screening only.** A false positive costs a real applicant a real
  job. This is a triage aid for human review, never a verdict.

## System

Standalone LoRA adapter. Requires `mistralai/Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1` loaded
first via PEFT.

## Implementation requirements

- **Training platform:** Adaption AutoScientist (cloud compute)
- **Base model size:** 46.7B total parameters / 12.9B active per token
- **Training method:** SFT + LoRA (attention projections only)
- **Training epochs:** 4 (88 optimizer steps)
- **Inference:** Needs GPU VRAM for Mixtral's full 46.7B footprint — sparse
  activation reduces compute, not memory, so all experts must be resident.
  4-bit quantization fits on ~24 GB.

---

# Model Characteristics

## Model initialization

Fine-tuned from `mistralai/Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1` using LoRA. Base weights
are frozen; only adapter weights are trained.

## Model stats

Read directly from the distributed `adapter_config.json` and `trainer_state.json`.

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Base model | Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1 |
| Base model size | 46.7B parameters (12.9B active per token) |
| LoRA rank (r) | 64 |
| LoRA alpha | 128 |
| LoRA dropout | 0 |
| Trainable modules | `q_proj`, `k_proj`, `v_proj`, `o_proj` (attention only) |
| Epochs / steps | 4 / 88 |
| Peak learning rate | 1e-4 (cosine) |
| Adapter size | 202 MB, 256 tensors |

**On the module selection.** This adapter touches attention projections only.
Mixtral is a mixture-of-experts model whose FFN experts (`w1`/`w2`/`w3`) hold
much of its parametric knowledge and are left untouched here — a narrower
configuration than an all-linear run would produce.

---

# Data Overview

## Training data

**Diagnostic + training set:** [EMSCAD Zero-Shot Headroom (Kaggle)](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/fernandosr85/emscad-zero-shot-headroom)

3,218 prompt/completion pairs derived from EMSCAD (Employment Scam Aegean
Dataset): 17,880 advertisements published through Workable 2012–2014, manually
annotated by Workable staff via quality-assurance procedures — 17,014 legitimate
and 866 fraudulent.

| Step | Detail |
|---|---|
| Label source | Human annotation, external to this project |
| Text fields | title, company_profile, description, requirements, benefits |
| Excluded | `has_company_logo`, `has_questions`, `telecommuting`, `salary_range` |
| Deduplication | 27.9% of fraudulent descriptions are exact duplicates vs 17.9% of legitimate ones; removed before splitting |
| Split | Grouped on normalized description, so template families cannot straddle train and holdout |
| Class balance | Oversampled to 22% fraud (natural: 4.10% in the train pool) |
| Hard negatives | 118 fraudulent ads (25.0% of positives) selected by 5-fold out-of-fold probability, boosted 3× |
| Completions | Kept verbatim, **not** platform-regenerated |

**On the 22% target.** Training at the natural 4.10% teaches the model to answer
`LEGITIMATE`; training at 50% teaches it to over-flag and destroys the
false-positive rate, which is the property worth protecting here. 22% is a
hypothesis about that tradeoff, and it is unverified until the holdout is scored.

**On hard-negative selection.** The first attempt selected them by the vocabulary
of the scams the base model missed. It failed: the legitimate baseline was drawn
from the 145-ad eval set, a word appearing in 1% of ads has a 23% chance of
appearing zero times in 145, and a `1e-3` floor in the lift denominator turned
that zero into `lift=133x`. `leveraging` and `aptitude` were promoted to scam
signals and 49% of all fraud matched — a hard-case selector selecting half the
corpus. Out-of-fold probability replaced it: a fraudulent ad that a linear model
trained *without* it still scores as legitimate is hard by definition.

**On the platform's regenerated completions.** Adaptive Data produces its own
answer for each row rather than transforming the supplied label. On a 47-row
sample it reached recall 28.6% against the base model's measured 30.8% — the same
operating point, which is what it is designed to do. Training used the original
completions, so this does not affect the adapter. It is noted because several of
the disagreements are cases where the platform read the *text* correctly and
EMSCAD's label encodes information the text does not carry (see *A text-only
ceiling* below).

## Evaluation data

210-row holdout, group-split on normalized description, published in the
diagnostic dataset. Fraud-boosted so recall is estimable at all — a natural
150-row sample contains about 7 fraudulent ads. Precision is derived
analytically at the true 4.84% base rate rather than measured on the boosted
sample, which overstates it by roughly 3.5×.

---

# Evaluation Results

## Summary — Adaption AutoScientist win rate

| Metric | Base | Adapted |
|---|---|---|
| Win rate — in-domain (this dataset) | 52 | 48 |

**Win rate is the wrong instrument for this task, and the number shows it.** The
metric asks a judge to *prefer* one response over another. Both responses here
are a single word drawn from a set of two: when both are right, or both wrong,
there is nothing to prefer and the judge is scoring noise. 48 against 52 is a
coin landing four points off even.

## Training convergence

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Train loss | 2.7852 → 0.0030 |
| Eval loss | 0.0921 → 0.0243 |
| LoRA `B` matrices | 128/128 trained (median Frobenius norm 0.231) |

The final loss rules out the obvious failure mode. On a 22%-fraud mixture, a
model that always answers `LEGITIMATE` bottoms out near 0.589; one that predicts
the base rate without discriminating bottoms out at 0.527. The observed 0.0030 is
**176× below** that floor, and eval loss tracked train loss without diverging.
The adapter learned to discriminate on its training distribution.

## Zero-shot baselines on the same holdout

Text-only, precision derived at the 4.84% base rate.

| Method | Fraud precision | Fraud recall | Fraud F1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Majority ("always legitimate") | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.000 |
| Published Random Forest (used metadata) | 0.282 | 0.751 | 0.410 |
| Claude zero-shot (text-only) | 0.694 | 0.308 | 0.426 |
| TF-IDF + SGD (text-only) | 0.757 | 0.846 | **0.799** |
| **This adapter** | — | — | **not measured** |

The headroom survived three independent attempts to explain it away: forced
binary answer (F1 0.409), probability plus threshold sweep (best 0.395), and
probability without the base-rate anchor (best 0.329, AUROC 0.799 vs 0.767 —
a +0.032 difference, 0.86 standard errors, indistinguishable from zero).
Thresholding does not help and removing the prior does not help. The ceiling is
not the prompt's framing.

A linear classifier over ~11.5k rows beats the frontier model by 37 points and
beats the published Random Forest that had the metadata.

## A text-only ceiling

The base model reaches recall 0.308 at FPR 0.007 — near-perfect on what it
flags, silent on the rest. Two observations suggest this is not simple failure.

**EMSCAD's fraud label encodes provenance, not text.** Several fraudulent ads
are scam operators reposting real job advertisements verbatim. Checked against
EMSCAD's own metadata:

| Advertisement | Label | `has_company_logo` | `company_profile` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Civil Engineer II (**AECOM**) | FRAUDULENT | 0 | missing |
| Engineering Senior Supervisor | FRAUDULENT | 0 | missing |
| Mechanical Technician (**Aker Solutions**) | FRAUDULENT | 1 | present |

AECOM and Aker Solutions are real companies and the descriptions are detailed,
plausible job specs. The *text* is legitimate; what is fraudulent is who posted
it. No text-only model can see that, and neither can a human reading only the ad.

The converse also occurs. One advertisement labelled `LEGITIMATE` carries a scam
operator's handle inline in the description (`ayobamijegsonmoney:` mid-sentence,
amid misspelled role titles). On that row the gold label is the questionable one.

**A linear model finds signal the frontier model does not.** TF-IDF reaches
recall 0.846 against Claude's 0.308, both text-only. The signal *is* in the text,
but it appears to be largely **lexical and distributional** — templated scam
vocabulary repeated across the 2012–2014 fraudulent class — rather than semantic.
A model reading for meaning misses it; a model counting tokens catches it.

**The risk this creates:** the adapter may be learning 2012–2014 lexical
artifacts that do not transfer to contemporary scam advertisements. Measuring
holdout recall would establish in-distribution performance only.

## Usage limitations

- Holdout recall and FPR unmeasured; the model is unvalidated for deployment.
- **Text-only ceiling.** Part of the fraud signal is provenance rather than text;
  no text-only model recovers those cases.
- **Possible lexical overfitting.** TF-IDF at recall 0.846 suggests much of the
  recoverable signal is period vocabulary. Generalization is untested.
- Trained on 2012–2014 advertisements.
- Screening aid for human review, not an automated decision.

## Ethics

Automated fraud screening acts on people. A false positive removes a real
applicant from a real job, which is why the false-positive rate is reported
alongside recall throughout the diagnostic and why the training mixture is
calibrated at 22% rather than balanced: a balanced set produces a model that
over-flags, and over-flagging has a victim.

The base model's failure mode is worth naming, because an adapter inherits the
context it was trained in. Asked for P(scam) as a number, **42.4% of all ads and
27.7% of actual scams receive exactly 0.05** — with no prior stated in the
prompt. The model does not express uncertainty as an intermediate value; it
returns a default that reads as a confident low probability. At threshold 0.70 it
is perfectly precise on what it flags and silent on three quarters of the scams.
That is a knowledge-boundary failure, not a calibration one, and it is the gap
this adapter was built to close.

---

## Credits

- **Fine-tuning platform:** [Adaption](https://adaptionlabs.ai) — AutoScientist & Adaptive Data
- **Challenge:** [AutoScientist Challenge 2026](https://adaptionlabs.ai/blog/autoscientist-challenge) — HR category
- **Source dataset:** [EMSCAD / Real or Fake Job Posting Prediction](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/shivamb/real-or-fake-fake-jobposting-prediction)
- **Source paper:** Vidros, Kolias, Kambourakis & Akoglu, *Automatic Detection of Online Recruitment Frauds*, Future Internet 9(1), 2017 — [MDPI](https://www.mdpi.com/1999-5903/9/1/6)
- **Kaggle diagnostic:** [emscad-zero-shot-headroom](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/fernandosr85/emscad-zero-shot-headroom)
- **Author:** Fernando Rodrigues · [Kaggle: fernandosr85](https://www.kaggle.com/fernandosr85)

    torch_dtype=torch.float16,
    device_map="auto",
)

model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(
    base_model,
    "/kaggle/input/emscad-employment-scam-detection-adapter/other/default/1",
)
# The task instruction used during training (one word, no explanation)
PROMPT = """You are reviewing a job advertisement submitted to an applicant tracking system, to decide whether it is a legitimate posting or an employment scam.

Employment scams typically aim to harvest personal data or money from applicants. Roughly 5% of postings in this system are fraudulent, so most ads you see are legitimate.

)

models.description:
# Model Summary

This model predicts a student's exam score based on the number of hours they studied using a **Linear Regression** algorithm from Scikit-learn.

The model is intended for educational purposes, demonstrating a simple supervised machine learning regression task. It learns the linear relationship between study hours and exam scores from a small dataset and predicts the expected score for new inputs.

**Architecture:** Linear Regression (`sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression`)

**Input:** Number of study hours (float)

**Output:** Predicted exam score (float)

**Training Dataset:** Student Scores dataset (`student_scores.csv`)

**Evaluation Metrics:** Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) and R² Score

---

# Usage

Load the model using Joblib and provide the number of study hours as input.

```python
import joblib
import pandas as pd

model = joblib.load("Student_Hours_Marks_Predictor.pkl")

hours = 6.5

prediction = model.predict(pd.DataFrame({"Hours": [hours]}))

print(f"Predicted Score: {prediction[0]:.2f}")
```

### Input

| Feature | Type  | Description             |
| ------- | ----- | ----------------------- |
| Hours   | float | Number of hours studied |

### Output

| Output          | Type  | Description                 |
| --------------- | ----- | --------------------------- |
| Predicted Score | float | Estimated examination score |

### Known Limitations

* Supports only a single input feature (study hours).
* Assumes a linear relationship between study hours and scores.
* Predictions should not be interpreted as actual academic performance.
* Not intended for grading, admissions, or educational decision-making.

---

# System

This is a standalone Scikit-learn regression model.

**Dependencies**

* Python 3.10+
* Scikit-learn
* Pandas
* Joblib
* NumPy

The model accepts a single numerical input and returns one numerical prediction. No external services or APIs are required.

---

# Implementation Requirements

### Training Environment

* Language: Python
* Framework: Scikit-learn
* Model: Linear Regression
* Serialization: Joblib

### Hardware

The model was trained on a standard consumer CPU. No GPU or specialized hardware is required.

### Compute Requirements

Training takes less than one second on modern hardware.

Inference is nearly instantaneous (typically less than one millisecond per prediction).

Energy consumption was not measured.

---

# Model Characteristics

## Model Initialization

The model was trained **from scratch** using Scikit-learn's Linear Regression implementation.

No pre-trained weights or transfer learning were used.

---

## Model Stats

* Algorithm: Linear Regression
* Number of Features: 1
* Number of Outputs: 1
* Number of Parameters: 2 (slope and intercept)
* Model Size: Very small (few KB)
* Latency: Near real-time

---

## Other Details

* Not pruned
* Not quantized
* No differential privacy techniques were applied

---

# Data Overview

The dataset contains paired observations of study hours and corresponding exam scores.

It is a small educational dataset commonly used to demonstrate regression algorithms.

---

## Training Data

Features:

* Hours Studied

Target:

* Exam Score

Preprocessing:

* No missing values
* No normalization or feature engineering
* Random 80/20 train-test split

---

## Demographic Groups

The dataset contains no demographic information such as age, gender, ethnicity, nationality, or socioeconomic background.

No demographic analysis was performed.

---

## Evaluation Data

Train/Test Split:

* Training: 80%
* Testing: 20%

Random State:

* 42

The training and testing data were randomly sampled from the same dataset.

---

# Evaluation Results

## Summary

Model performance was evaluated using:

* Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
* Coefficient of Determination (R²)

These metrics provide an indication of prediction error and goodness of fit.

---

## Subgroup Evaluation Results

No subgroup evaluation was performed because the dataset contains no subgroup attributes.

---

## Fairness

Since the dataset contains no demographic information, fairness metrics were not evaluated.

The model should not be used in scenarios where fairness across demographic groups is required.

---

## Usage Limitations

This model is intended for:

* Machine learning education
* Regression demonstrations
* Beginner projects
* Research experiments

It should **not** be used for:

* Academic grading
* Scholarship selection
* Student evaluation
* High-stakes educational decisions

The model ignores many real-world factors that influence academic performance, including attendance, prior knowledge, sleep, motivation, teaching quality, learning style, and exam difficulty.

---

## Ethics

This model was developed solely for educational and demonstration purposes.

Potential risks include overinterpreting predictions as indicators of actual student ability or future academic success.

Users should understand that study hours alone cannot accurately determine academic performance, and predictions should only be used as illustrative examples of linear regression.

instances.overview:
# Variations

This release contains a single baseline implementation using **Scikit-learn's Linear Regression** algorithm.

Possible future variations of this model include:

* **Polynomial Regression** to capture non-linear relationships between study hours and exam scores.
* **Multiple Linear Regression** by incorporating additional features such as attendance, previous grades, sleep duration, assignment scores, and class participation.
* **Regularized Models** (Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet) to improve generalization on larger datasets.
* **Tree-Based Models** such as Decision Trees, Random Forests, and Gradient Boosting for handling more complex relationships.
* **Neural Network Regression** for larger and more feature-rich educational datasets.

The current model is intentionally simple, lightweight, and interpretable, making it well-suited for learning the fundamentals of regression and serving as a baseline for future experimentation and comparison.

# Example Usage Guide

## 1. Install Dependencies

```bash
pip install scikit-learn pandas joblib
```

---

## 2. Load the Model

```python
import joblib

model = joblib.load("Student_Hours_Marks_Predictor.pkl")
```

---

## 3. Make a Prediction

```python
import pandas as pd

hours = 8.5

prediction = model.predict(
    pd.DataFrame({"Hours": [hours]})
)

print(f"Predicted Score: {prediction[0]:.2f}")
```

Example Output:

```text
Predicted Score: 86.74
```

*(The exact value depends on the trained model.)*

---

## 4. Predict Multiple Students

```python
import pandas as pd

students = pd.DataFrame({
    "Hours": [2, 4.5, 6, 8, 10]
})

predictions = model.predict(students)

students["Predicted Score"] = predictions

print(students)
```
